SLIDES:
I’ve just listened to a really interesting programme on the radio.

Present Perfect: it finished a moment ago and it still matters now. No time word.

He lost his mother when he was a boy.

Past Simple: the sentence says when. Finished time, finished action.

He has recently found her again after twenty-five years.

Present Perfect: the result is true now — he has her back.

He travelled to Khandwa and found his old house.

Past Simple: the story moves. Once you start the story, you stay in the past.

Have you ever been to India? — Yes, I went there in 2019.

The question is about your life (Present Perfect). The answer gives the year, so it turns into Past Simple.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Finished time, or your life so far

Both tenses talk about the past. Only one of them says when.

Read these four sentences from the recording in stage 5.
  • I’ve just listened to a really interesting programme.
  • He lost his mother when he was a boy.
  • He has recently found her again after twenty-five years.
  • He fell asleep and woke up fourteen hours later.
Some of these sentences tell you exactly when it happened. Which tense do they use?
The choice: does the sentence say when?
Present Perfect — unfinished timePast Simple — finished time
PositiveHe has found his mother.He found her in 2011.
NegativeI haven’t seen that film.I didn’t see it last night.
QuestionHave you ever been to India?When did you go to India?
Short answerYes, I have. / No, I haven’t.Yes, I did. / No, I didn’t.
Time wordsever, never, just, recently, in my lifeyesterday, in 2010, last week, when I was five, two years ago
What it doesconnects the past to now — the result matters todayputs the event in a closed box of time
Past Simple recycledOnce a story starts, it stays in the Past Simple: He fell asleep, woke up in Kolkata and lived on the streets.
The rules that matter
  • Form: have / has + past participle. been, done, seen, found, lived, moved. Irregular verbs have a third form — learn it with the other two.
  • If the sentence names a finished time (yesterday, in 2010, when I was five), you must use the Past Simple. This is the rule that decides almost every exam item.
  • Use the Present Perfect for experience in your life so far: Have you ever eaten horse meat?
  • A very common pattern: the first question is Present Perfect, the answer moves to Past Simple. — Have you been to Astana? — Yes, I went there last summer.
  • for and since also work with this tense (I’ve lived here for ten years). They come back properly in Unit 12.
Full grammar reference — Present Perfect Simple and Past Simple

Form

Present Perfecthave / has + past participle: I have lived · she has found
NegativeI haven’t seen it · he hasn’t arrived
QuestionHave you ever been to India?
Short answersYes, I have. / No, he hasn’t.
Past Simple, for contrastI saw it yesterday. · When did you go?

Spelling and sound

The third form of irregular verbs must be learned with the other two: go – went – gone, see – saw – seen, be – was – been.

When and why we use it

  • The Past Simple is used when the sentence says, or clearly implies, when it happened.
  • The Present Perfect connects the past to now: experience in your life so far, or a past action whose result matters today.
  • A very common pattern: the question is Present Perfect, the answer moves to Past Simple. — Have you been to Astana? — Yes, I went last summer.
  • Been = went and came back. Gone = went and is still there.

Signal words

Present Perfect: ever, never, recently, in my life, so far. Past Simple: yesterday, in 2010, last week, when I was five, two years ago.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I have seen him yesterday. → I saw him yesterday.A finished time forces the Past Simple.
  • I am here since 2019. → I have been here since 2019.Started in the past, still true.
  • Have you went there? → Have you been there?The third form after have.
  • When have you arrived? → When did you arrive?When asks for a finished time.

Don’t confuse it with

If you can add yesterday or a year to the sentence, use the Past Simple. If the time is open (ever, so far, this week), use the Present Perfect.
